summary:
We developed ARES TRAIL, an interactive Marswalk planning prototype that helps users explore Martian terrain, compare possible routes, and examine the evidence behind their choices.

For the “Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map” challenge, we combined NASA data from Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, Mars Global Surveyor, and Perseverance into one workspace. Users can switch between 2D maps and 3D terrain, compare distance-focused and terrain-aware paths, inspect checkpoint imagery and observation dates, record notes, and export mission reports.

Detailed planning focuses on Jezero Crater, while coarser datasets support regional exploration elsewhere on Mars.

ARES TRAIL matters because a route is more useful when people can understand its terrain, inspect its sources, and recognize what remains unknown. Designed for education and mission-planning research, it makes planetary data easier to explore while clearly distinguishing measured information from calculations and assumptions. It is a prototype, not an operational astronaut safety system.
details:
We built ARES TRAIL — Marswalk Mission Planner around a question: before someone walks across Mars, how can they understand the terrain ahead and the evidence behind their planned route?

Created for the NASA Space Apps challenge “Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map,” ARES TRAIL brings data from several Mars missions into one interactive workspace. Users can explore the surface, compare possible routes, inspect scientific observations, and record what still needs a closer look.

How it works

ARES TRAIL combines CTX imagery and stereo elevation data from NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, HiRISE observations, Mars Global Surveyor MOLA topography, and published Perseverance Mastcam-Z panoramas.

For Jezero Crater, we use elevation data with a 20-meter source resolution, grouped into planning cells of approximately 100 meters. We calculate slope and terrain relief, then use an A* pathfinding algorithm to generate routes. Users can compare a distance-focused path with one that gives more weight to terrain conditions. Both follow the same exclusion rules.

We wanted users to be able to question the route. Clicking a numbered checkpoint opens its coordinates, terrain measurements, available imagery, observation dates, and source references. Users can examine the surroundings, write inspection notes, and export those notes with the plan.

The workspace includes interactive 2D and 3D views, elevation and sampled-slope profiles, route comparison charts, and printable mission reports.

Users can also explore Gale Crater, Olympus Mons, or a region chosen through custom coordinates. Those areas use much coarser MOLA data, so we clearly label their routes as broad reconnaissance corridors. They do not provide enough detail to judge individual walking hazards.

Why we built it

Mars data comes from different instruments, missions, and archives. Understanding how those pieces fit together can take considerable effort. We wanted to make selected datasets easier to explore together and make route decisions easier to explain.

For example, a user might notice a detour and ask: Is the direct path steeper? What can we see in the orbital image? Is there enough information to assess this crossing?

ARES TRAIL helps users investigate those questions. We see its immediate value in planetary science education, exploration training, and mission-planning research. It can also give scientific and technical teams a shared view of a proposed traverse.

It remains a research prototype. It is not ready to guide astronauts or determine whether an actual Marswalk is safe.

What we used

We built the interface with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Leaflet handles the interactive 2D map, and Three.js renders the terrain in 3D.

Our Python processing tools include NumPy, SciPy, Rasterio, Pillow, and Requests. We use Matplotlib to create evaluation figures. An optional Flask backend provides coordinate-based route summaries, while terrain-aware routing runs in the browser.

We use Playwright for browser testing, GitHub for source control, and Vercel for hosting. OpenAI Codex assisted with development, debugging, testing, and documentation. The project does not connect to physical hardware or live spacecraft telemetry.

What makes our approach different

The part we focused on most was the connection between a route and its supporting evidence. A user can calculate a path, inspect observations along it, document their reasoning, and keep that context in the exported report.

The map, 3D view, checkpoints, and reports all reflect the same current plan. We also show nearby terrain-based investigation candidates as places worth examining, with their geological meaning left unconfirmed.

What we considered

We paid close attention to how the interface communicates certainty. Real observations, calculated measurements, and planning assumptions have different roles, and we label them accordingly. We show missing coverage and distinguish the original data resolution from the resolution of a displayed preview.

We also worked on making a complex tool approachable. Frequently used controls stay accessible, advanced settings can be expanded when needed, and large visualizations load only when requested. Source manifests retain product references and checksums so the data can be traced.

There are important limits. Our terrain grids cannot resolve individual rocks or narrow obstacles. Walking-time and oxygen estimates use simplified distance-based assumptions and exclude the return journey. Regional data is too coarse for walking-scale decisions.

We want users to leave with a clearer understanding of a proposed route: what the available measurements tell them, what observations support it, and what still needs to be surveyed.
